The paper gives the update rules as standard MAML over soft-prompt parameters θ. In the extracted text, most math symbols are garbled (shown as "�"). I reconstructed them below using standard MAML notation. The parts that survive in the text are θ, α, the subscript i, and the superscripts "support" and "query".

**Inner loop (task-specific prompt update), which uses the support set** (p. 2, §3.2):

  θᵢ′ = θ − α ∇_θ ℒ_{Tᵢ}(f_θ ; Dᵢ^support)

- α is the inner-loop learning rate, and f_θ is the LLM conditioned on the prompt θ (p. 2).
- Page 1 gives a shorter version, θᵢ′ = θ − α ∇_θ ℒ_{Tᵢ}(θ). It also says each task Tᵢ is adapted using a few labeled interactions (x, y) ∈ Dᵢ^support (p. 1).

**Outer loop (meta-objective across tasks), which uses the query set** (p. 2, §3.2):

  min_θ Σᵢ ℒ_{Tᵢ}(f_{θᵢ′} ; Dᵢ^query)

- θ is chosen so that performance after adaptation on Dᵢ^query is maximized (p. 1).
- The loss is computed with the adapted prompt θᵢ′, but the minimization is over the shared initialization θ (p. 1–2).

**About the data splits:**
- Each user task Tᵢ has a support set and a query set. The goal is low loss on the query set after a few updates on the support set (p. 2, §3.1).
- During meta-training, each user has 1–5 interactions in the support set and 1–5 in the query set (p. 2, §3.4).
- At test time, the support set has K ∈ {1, 3, 5} interactions, used only for adapting the prompt. The model is then evaluated on a separate set of unseen interactions from the same user (p. 3, §4.1).
- The LLM itself stays frozen. Gradients are computed only for the soft prompt P ∈ ℝ^{l×d} (p. 2, §3.3; p. 3, §4.4).
